title: ML in Production: From Models to Systems
oneLiner: A model that works in a notebook is a component; a product needs a whole system around it, and that system decides what users actually experience.

what.html:
An ML system is everything around the model: the app and its users, data collection, storage, the serving API, payments, logging and monitoring. The model may be the heart of the product or a small add-on, and big systems often contain many models that feed each other.

Everyday versionA car engine on a test bench is impressive, but it isn't a car. You still need a body, brakes, dashboard, fuel system and service schedule, and if the engine misfires, the rest of the car must keep you safe.

why.html:
• Real data is noisy, users expect speed, and compute costs money: a good model alone doesn't make a business.
  • The model code is a small part of the total code; the "glue" around it causes most production problems.
  • Models make mistakes, and the system must stop those mistakes from hurting users.
  • The world changes, so a model that is never monitored slowly gets worse.

how.title: Prototype to product
how.html: A researcher's transcription model beats generic tools on technical vocabulary. Turning it into a start-up adds noisy audio, deadlines of minutes (or real-time captions), GPU bills, a website with payments, fragile retraining, team communication and fairness issues with dialects. Most of the work is engineering beyond ML.

how.title: Think in systems, not models
how.html: Model-centric: tune features and hyperparameters for accuracy. System-centric: improve data, infrastructure, deployment and user experience so the whole thing works reliably. Both matter, but users only meet the system.

how.title: The hidden iceberg
how.html: In production, the pipeline doesn't end at evaluation: you monitor the model on live data, pick new data for retraining and update the model regularly. And the ML code is a small box surrounded by configuration, data collection, feature extraction, verification, serving and monitoring.

how.title: ML as one component among many
how.html: In a transcription service ML is the core; in tax software, audit-risk prediction is just an add-on. Either way it sits next to ordinary components, and large products have many ML parts: a labelling tool, an inference service, a feature store, pipelines and a model monitor.

how.title: Two tracks, one system
how.html: Software work (requirements → design → build → test → operate) runs alongside data-science experiments (is ML suitable? → explore data, build models → integrate → operate). Systems thinking joins them: what does the whole system need, and what happens when the ML part is wrong?

how.title: Predict, generate, act
how.html: Predictive AI forecasts from past data. Generative AI creates content from plain instructions. Agentic AI takes a goal, plans steps, uses tools and keeps improving until it's done. Generative AI needs far more compute, data and elastic infrastructure than predictive AI.

how.title: Cloud-native foundations
how.html: Containers, microservices and orchestration (Kubernetes) let ML workloads scale up and down reliably on public, private or hybrid clouds, from GPUs at the bottom to ML pipelines and apps at the top.

how.title: Lessons from real systems
how.html: A self-driving stack uses 28 models whose outputs feed each other, with code doing fusion, validation and decisions, so one failure can travel all the way to the steering. Large companies follow a nine-stage ML workflow full of feedback loops, with data at its centre, new roles, and SE practices like versioning, CI/CD and monitoring.

demo.html: A photo app auto-tags images. Slide the review threshold up: fewer wrong tags reach users, but humans must check more photos. Lower the model quality and see how the same system design has to absorb the extra mistakes. This trade-off is a system decision, not a model decision.

example.html:
Transcription start-up, six months in. Accuracy on medical calls is excellent, but customers complain about 40-minute turnaround, a GPU bill larger than revenue, and errors with regional accents. The fixes are system fixes: batch long recordings overnight and stream only live captions, cache common vocabulary, add an accent-specific evaluation set and monitor errors per dialect, and automate retraining so model updates stop causing outages.

Supplementary The same pattern appears in a bank: the fraud model is 1% of the code, while streaming features, rules, case-management UI and alerting make up the rest.

misunderstandings: A better model always means a better product.
Only if the model is the bottleneck; often latency, data quality or UX matter more.
The ML code is most of the work.
It's a small part; data collection, serving and monitoring dominate.
The system must contain them with thresholds, reviews, fallbacks and monitoring.
Agentic AI is just a smarter chatbot.
Agents pursue goals by planning, using tools and acting in loops.
Once deployed, a model keeps its accuracy.
Drift makes unmonitored models degrade over time.
takeaways: Prototype → production needs engineering far beyond the model: data, latency, cost, product, pipelines, team, monitoring.
Think system-centric: the model is one component among many, core or auxiliary.
In production the pipeline adds monitoring, data selection and regular updates; most code is hidden 'glue'.
Plan for ML mistakes: errors propagate, so contain them with thresholds, humans and fallbacks.
Predictive, generative and agentic AI differ in purpose and infrastructure; real systems combine many models in iterative, data-centred workflows.
thirty: An ML model is a component; an ML system is everything around it: UI, data collection, storage, serving, payments, logging and monitoring. Taking a research model to production raises problems the notebook never saw: noisy real data, latency targets, compute cost, a product to build, fragile retraining and fairness issues. In production the pipeline continues after evaluation: you monitor the model on live data, select new data and retrain regularly. ML code is a small fraction of the system, and the hidden glue causes most failures. ML can be the core of a product or an add-on, and large systems combine many models, as a self-driving stack does with 28. Because models make mistakes, the system must contain them. Finally, predictive, generative and agentic AI differ in what they do and what infrastructure they need.

opts: Data, infrastructure, deployment and user experience end to end
